extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, economists, patent policy scholars, patent practitioners, and policymakers interested in continuation practice and standard-essential patents (SEPs)
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical analysis of how continuation applications are used to obtain claims that read on published standards (SEPs), and the relation between late claiming, claim text, examination outcomes, and litigation. Uses matching, difference-in-differences, and text-similarity measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-statutory double patenting rejections as proxy for claim broadening
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent examiners may reject a claim if the same inventor has disclosed 'patentably indistinct' claims in a previous application. This non-statutory (obviousness-type) double patenting rejection is taken as a proxy for 'claim broadening' or 'claim tailoring' (as opposed to claiming new and distinct uses of the original invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicants use continuations to draft claims that read on standards, expect more non-statutory double-patenting rejections for SEP continuations filed after standard publication than before. Construct matched samples (same year, art unit, examiner), restrict to continuations with full examination histories, estimate linear probability models (outcome=double patenting rejection ×100). Cluster standard errors by patent family. See Table 4 and accompanying notes for implementation details and sample exclusions (e.g. exclude continuations filed before 2008 or disposed after June 2017).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-language convergence measured by Jaccard similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure similarity of claims across pairs of applications linked to the same standard via a Jaccard index: number of common keywords in the claims divided by total keywords, multiplied by 100.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare Jaccard similarity for post-standard continuations (J_post) versus pre-standard parent applications (J_pre). Retain pairs where both continuations and parents have at least 10 keywords and drop pairs where the two continuations claim priority to the same parent. Use OLS regressions, pair fixed effects, and controls (filing year effects, art-unit-by-examiner effects, log number of independent claims, words per independent claim). Interpret greater post-publication similarity as evidence that applicants draft claims to cover standards (see Table 5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation indicator as outcome for SEP value/controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcome equals one if a SEP is litigated at least once in a U.S. district court before end of 2018 (multiplied by 100 for interpretation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key explanatory variables: indicator for continuation application, indicator for being filed after standard publication, and filing lag (difference in years between SEP filing month and standard publication month). Include issue-year, filing-year, art-unit, and examiner fixed effects. Estimate linear probability models; cluster standard errors by patent family. Use to assess association between late claiming/prosecution delay and higher litigation rates (see Table 6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of SEP for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: SEPs include U.S. utility patent applications declared essential for a standard, as well as all their parent and child applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a robustness check, consider an alternative SEP definition that includes only patents/applications explicitly mentioned in SSO disclosure letters (i.e., excluding undeclared U.S. family members). Use consistent earliest-standard linking to define pre- and post-standard families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matched-control sampling on art unit, filing year, and examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: Match each SEP continuation with a non-SEP continuation filed in the same year and assigned to the same art unit and examiner (1-to-1 match without replacement, break ties at random).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This matching yields a sample designed to be technologically similar and exposed to similar examination environments. Reporting: matching covered ~93% of SEP continuations after specified exclusions. Use matched sample when estimating probability of double-patenting rejections and other contrasts (see Table 4 notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample restrictions to observe full examination history
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude continuations filed before 2008 or disposed after June 2017 in order to observe full examination histories from administrative data sources (e.g., Lu et al. 2017).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These temporal restrictions ensure availability of office action histories and enable construction of variables such as first non-final rejection, first final rejection, first notice of allowance, and continuation timing statistics. Resulting sample sizes (e.g. 10,588 continuation applications) are reported with regression models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative outcome: any child application versus continuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcome variable can be defined as an indicator for any type of child application — including continuations-in-part (CIPs), divisionals, and reissues — as opposed to just continuations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this alternative outcome in robustness checks to test sensitivity of results to how 'child' filings are defined (see Table A5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls for observable application characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Include controls that may be related to both SEP status and continuation propensity, such as filing year effects, art-unit-by-examiner effects, number of independent claims, words per independent claim, and application type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding these controls helps address confounding; however, they may reduce sample size due to missing data. Use in regressions of claim similarity, continuation probability, and litigation to check robustness (see Table A6 and Table 5 model 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate anticipation/pre-trends with leads and event-study
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate models that include leads of an indicator equal to one for SEPs in the quarter of standard publication to measure anticipation effects and pre-trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include up to four leads and implement event-study specifications; report results in robustness tables (Table A7) and figures. Interpret significant leads cautiously as possible anticipation or pre-trend violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address DID staggered-treatment bias using recent estimators
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize potential bias in difference-in-differences (DID) designs with heterogeneous effects and staggered treatment timing and check robustness using newer unbiased estimators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply estimators proposed by de Chaisemartin & D’Haultfœuille (2020a,b), Callaway & Sant’Anna (2020), Sun & Abraham (2020), and Borusyak et al. (2021) to validate baseline DID and event-study estimates (see Tables A15–A17 and Figures A4–A6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Piecewise constant hazard models for rare continuation outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Because continuation is a rare outcome, estimate piecewise constant hazard models where the outcome is the probability of continuation conditional on not having any prior continuations, removing applications after the first observed continuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this approach to account for time-to-event structure and rarity of outcome; report results in Tables A8–A10.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing lag as continuous measure of prosecution delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure prosecution delay as the difference (in years) between the filing month of the SEP and the month of standard publication; negative values indicate SEPs filed before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include filing-lag as a continuous explanatory variable in litigation regressions to estimate change in litigation probability per year of filing lag (e.g., ~0.25 percentage points per year). Pair with post-standard dummy and continuation indicators to disentangle timing versus continuation effects (see Table 6 columns 2 and 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of double patenting rejection statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-statutory double patenting rejections often occur when an applicant seeks to change the scope of an earlier claim (e.g., expanding it by removing limitations); use these rejections as evidence of claim modification rather than wholly new claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare rates for post-standard SEP continuations versus matched non-SEP continuations and pre-standard SEPs. Report percentage-point differences and relative increases with baseline probabilities (e.g., post-standard SEPs ~8 percentage points more likely; 15% increase relative to 50% baseline).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pair fixed effects to control for unobserved pair-level heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing claim similarity between post-standard continuations and their pre-standard parents, include pair fixed effects to control for all common characteristics of the pre- and post-standard applications in a pair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pair FE substantially increases R-squared and accounts for shared family-level attributes; combine with application-level controls for robustness (see Table 5 columns 2–3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cluster standard errors by patent family
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard errors in regression models should be clustered by patent family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clustering by family accounts for within-family correlation in outcomes (used throughout analyses, e.g., Tables 4–6). Report significance stars and standard errors in parentheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical criteria linking late claiming to litigation likelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical mechanisms: (i) plaintiffs more likely to assert patents for which infringement is easily proved (for SEPs, infringement typically argued by comparing claims to the standard); (ii) litigation more likely when stakes are higher, and patentees may invest in late claim drafting for more valuable inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these mechanisms to motivate empirical tests relating continuation status and filing lag to litigation outcomes; consider selection versus causal interpretation when continuations remain associated with higher litigation even after conditioning on filing lag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy remedies to limit opportunistic continuation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential policy options include adjusting USPTO fee schedules, adopting rules to limit lengthy continuation 'chains', adopting intervening-user rights to protect pre-adopters, and relying on prosecution laches in courts to render patents unenforceable for unreasonable delays. SSOs could also adopt clearer IP policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate trade-offs: policies might reduce opportunism but could lead to vaguer original claims or last-minute filings. Consider how interventions interact with applicants' incentives, and note empirical difficulty predicting counterfactual behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize other tools that delay claim drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuations are not the only way to delay claim drafting; applicants may use provisional applications, requests for continued examination (RCEs), divisionals, or deferred examination in other jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing delay and its effects, account for these alternative mechanisms and consider cross-jurisdictional differences where continuations are not available. Further research recommended to study combined use of these tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination-event timing statistics for continuations
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute for each office action (first non-final rejection, first final rejection, first notice of allowance): (i) percent of applications receiving the action; (ii) conditional probability of filing the first continuation within six months of the action; (iii) conditional probability that the first continuation is filed within six months from the action, given a continuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a six-month window because applicants have three months to reply to a rejection and can obtain up to three more months by paying a fee. These statistics help distinguish whether continuations are responses to rejections or are filed after notice of allowance (Table A2).
